import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.special import ndtr

Problem 1¶

Consider the multivariate normal random variable $\mathbf{X}$ with $\mathbb{E}[X_1] = 1$, $\mathbb{E}[X_2] = -2$, $\mathbb{E}[X_3] = 0$, $\textrm{Var}[X_1] = 2$, $\textrm{Var}[X_2] = 1$, $\textrm{Var}[X_3] = 4$, $\textrm{Corr}[X_1, X_2] = 0.6$, $\textrm{Corr}[X_1, X_3] = -0.3$ and $\textrm{Corr}[X_2, X_3] = 0.5$.

Part a¶

Simulate at least $10,000$ samples of $\mathbf{X}$. Calculate the sample means, sample variances and sample correlations of your simulations to confirm that they match the correct values.

Part b¶

Make three scatter plots of your simulations, one for each pair of variables. (E.g., plot $X_1$ vs $X_2$, then plot $X_1$ vs $X_3$, then plot $X_2$ vs $X_3$.)

Solution

Build the covariance matrix from variances and correlations:

$$\Sigma_{ij} = \mathrm{Corr}[X_i, X_j] \cdot \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[X_i]} \cdot \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[X_j]}$$

Then use the Cholesky decomposition $\Sigma = LL^T$ (where $L$ is lower triangular). If $\mathbf{Z} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, I)$ (iid standard normals), then:

$$\mathbf{X} = \boldsymbol{\mu} + L\mathbf{Z} \sim N(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma)$$

since $\mathrm{Cov}[L\mathbf{Z}] = L\,\mathrm{Cov}[\mathbf{Z}]\,L^T = L I L^T = \Sigma$.

In [2]:
np.random.seed(42)
n = 10_000

mu = np.array([1.0, -2.0, 0.0])
std = np.array([np.sqrt(2), 1.0, 2.0])

corr_mat = np.array([[1.0,  0.6, -0.3],
                     [0.6,  1.0,  0.5],
                     [-0.3, 0.5,  1.0]])

# Build covariance matrix: Cov[i,j] = Corr[i,j] * std[i] * std[j]
Sigma = corr_mat * np.outer(std, std)
print("Covariance matrix:\n", Sigma)

# Cholesky decomposition: Sigma = L @ L.T
L = np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma)
print("\nCholesky factor L:\n", L.round(4))

# Simulate: X = mu + L @ Z, Z ~ iid N(0,1)
Z = np.random.normal(0, 1, (n, 3))
X = mu + Z @ L.T

print("\nSample means:     ", X.mean(axis=0).round(4), " (exact: [1, -2, 0])")
print("Sample variances: ", X.var(axis=0).round(4),  " (exact: [2, 1, 4])")
print("Sample correlations:\n", np.corrcoef(X.T).round(4))
print("Exact correlations:\n", corr_mat)

Problem 2¶

Consider the multivariate normal random variable $X\sim N(\mathbf{0}, \Sigma)$, where

$$\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

Part a¶

What is the Cholesky decomposition of $\Sigma$? Explain why it might be problematic to generate samples of $X$ using this decomposition.

Part b¶

What is the pdf of $X$?

Part c¶

Generate $1,000$ samples of $X$ and make a scatter plot of the points. How does this plot relate to your answer from parts (a) and (b)?

Solution

Part a : Cholesky decomposition

For $\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, solve $LL^T = \Sigma$ for lower-triangular $L$:

$$L_{11} = \sqrt{\Sigma_{11}} = 1, \quad L_{21} = \Sigma_{21}/L_{11} = -1, \quad L_{22} = \sqrt{\Sigma_{22} - L_{21}^2} = \sqrt{1-1} = 0$$

$$L = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$$

The zero diagonal entry is problematic: $\Sigma$ is singular (positive semi-definite, not positive definite). Generating $\mathbf{X} = L\mathbf{Z}$ gives $X_1 = Z_1$ and $X_2 = -Z_1$, so all samples are forced onto the line $x_2 = -x_1$.

Part b : PDF of $X$

Since $\Sigma$ is singular, the distribution of $X$ is degenerate: there is no 2D pdf because all probability mass lies on the single line $x_2 = -x_1$. Along that line, $X_1 \sim N(0,1)$, so the distribution is fully described by a 1D standard normal.

Part c : Scatter plot

In [4]:
# X = L @ Z where L = [[1,0],[-1,0]], Z ~ N(0,I)
# So X1 = Z1, X2 = -Z1 : samples lie exactly on x2 = -x1
Z1 = np.random.normal(0, 1, 1000)
X2_p2 = np.column_stack([Z1, -Z1])

plt.figure(figsize=(5, 5))
plt.scatter(X2_p2[:, 0], X2_p2[:, 1], alpha=0.3, s=10)
x_line = np.linspace(-3, 3, 100)
plt.plot(x_line, -x_line, 'r--', label='$x_2 = -x_1$')
plt.xlabel("$X_1$")
plt.ylabel("$X_2$")
plt.title("Problem 2: Samples lie on $x_2 = -x_1$")
plt.legend()
plt.axis('equal')
plt.show()
print("All samples satisfy X2 = -X1:", np.allclose(X2_p2[:,0] + X2_p2[:,1], 0))

All samples satisfy X2 = -X1: True

Problem 3¶

In this problem, we will simulate correlated exponential random variables with the method of copulas.

Part a¶

Let $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ be standard normal random variables with correlation $\rho = 0.5$. Simulate $10,000$ samples of the random vector $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, Z_2)$. Make a scatter plot and histograms of your samples (i.e., plot $Z_1$ vs $Z_2$ and then plot the histogram of $Z_1$ and the histogram of $Z_2$) and calculate the sample correlation to confirm that they have the correct distribution.

Part b¶

For each of your samples from part (a), calculate the vector

$$\mathbf{U} = \begin{pmatrix} U_1 \\ U_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} F_Z(Z_1) \\ F_Z(Z_2) \end{pmatrix}$$

where $F_Z$ is the cdf of the standard normal distribution. (You can calculate $F_Z$ in python using scipy.special.ndtr().) Make a scatter plot and histograms of your samples (i.e., plot $U_1$ vs $U_2$ and then plot the histogram of $U_1$ and the histogram of $U_2$) and calculate the sample correlation. Do $U_1$ and $U_2$ appear to be uniformly distributed? Do they appear to be correlated? Does the correlation appear to be the same as $\textrm{Corr}[Z_1, Z_2]$?

Part c¶

For each of your samples from part (b), calculate the vector

$$\mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix} X_1 \\ X_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} F^{-1}(U_1) \\ F^{-1}(U_2) \end{pmatrix}$$

where $F$ is the cdf of an exponential random variable with parameter $\lambda = 1$. Make a scatter plot and histograms of your samples (i.e., plot $X_1$ vs $X_2$ and then plot this histogram of $X_1$ and the histogram of $X_2$) and calculate the sample correlation. Do $X_1$ and $X_2$ appear to be exponentially distributed? Do they appear to be correlated? Does the correlation appear to be the same as $\textrm{Corr}[Z_1, Z_2]$?

Part d¶

Repeat the sampling process from parts (a)-(b) for $\rho = -1$, $\rho = -0.9$, $\dotsc$, $\rho = 0.9$, \rho = 1$. That is, for each of the 21 values of $\rho$, simulate $10,000$ samples of $\mathbf{Z}$ with the appropriate correlation, then calculate

$$\mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix} F^{-1}(F_Z(Z_1)) \\ F^{-1}(F_Z(Z_2)) \end{pmatrix}$$

Plot $\textrm{Corr}[X_1, X_2]$ vs $\rho$.

Solution

Part a : Generate $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, Z_2)$ with $\mathrm{Corr}[Z_1, Z_2] = 0.5$ using Cholesky:

$$\Sigma_Z = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & 1\end{pmatrix} = LL^T, \qquad \mathbf{Z} = L\mathbf{W}, \quad \mathbf{W} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, I)$$

In [5]:
# Part a: Z1, Z2 ~ N(0,1) with correlation rho=0.5 via Cholesky
rho = 0.5
Sigma_z = np.array([[1.0, rho], [rho, 1.0]])
L_z = np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma_z)
Z = np.random.normal(0, 1, (10_000, 2)) @ L_z.T

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4))
axes[0].scatter(Z[:, 0], Z[:, 1], alpha=0.1, s=5)
axes[0].set_title("$Z_1$ vs $Z_2$")
axes[1].hist(Z[:, 0], bins=50)
axes[1].set_title("Histogram of $Z_1$")
axes[2].hist(Z[:, 1], bins=50)
axes[2].set_title("Histogram of $Z_2$")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"Sample correlation: {np.corrcoef(Z.T)[0,1]:.4f}  (exact: {rho})")

Sample correlation: 0.4910  (exact: 0.5)

Part b : Apply the probability integral transform $U_i = F_Z(Z_i) = \Phi(Z_i)$.

By the PIT, if $Z_i$ is continuous with CDF $\Phi$, then $U_i = \Phi(Z_i) \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$. The $U_i$ retain the dependence structure of $Z$ but have uniform marginals : this is the Gaussian copula.

Note: $\mathrm{Corr}[U_1, U_2] \neq \mathrm{Corr}[Z_1, Z_2]$ in general, since the CDF transform is nonlinear.

In [6]:
# Part b: U = (Phi(Z1), Phi(Z2)) -- uniform marginals
U = ndtr(Z)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4))
axes[0].scatter(U[:, 0], U[:, 1], alpha=0.1, s=5)
axes[0].set_title("$U_1$ vs $U_2$")
axes[1].hist(U[:, 0], bins=50)
axes[1].set_title("Histogram of $U_1$")
axes[2].hist(U[:, 1], bins=50)
axes[2].set_title("Histogram of $U_2$")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
corr_u = np.corrcoef(U.T)[0,1]
print(f"Sample correlation of U: {corr_u:.4f}")

Sample correlation of U: 0.4673

Part c : Apply the inverse CDF of $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ to each $U_i$.

For $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$: $F(x) = 1 - e^{-x}$, so $F^{-1}(u) = -\ln(1-u)$.

$$X_i = F^{-1}(U_i) = -\ln(1-U_i) \sim \mathrm{Exp}(1)$$

The marginals of $X$ are exponential, but $X_1$ and $X_2$ remain correlated because $U_1, U_2$ were correlated. However, $\mathrm{Corr}[X_1, X_2] \neq \rho$ since the nonlinear transforms change linear correlation.

In [7]:
# Part c: X = F_Exp^{-1}(U) where F_Exp(x) = 1 - e^{-x}, so F^{-1}(u) = -ln(1-u)
X_cop = -np.log(1 - U)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4))
axes[0].scatter(X_cop[:, 0], X_cop[:, 1], alpha=0.1, s=5)
axes[0].set_title("$X_1$ vs $X_2$")
axes[1].hist(X_cop[:, 0], bins=50)
axes[1].set_title("Histogram of $X_1$")
axes[2].hist(X_cop[:, 1], bins=50)
axes[2].set_title("Histogram of $X_2$")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
corr_x = np.corrcoef(X_cop.T)[0,1]
print(f"Sample correlation of X: {corr_x:.4f}")

Sample correlation of X: 0.4604

Part d : Sweep $\rho \in \{-1, -0.9, \ldots, 0.9, 1\}$ and compute $\mathrm{Corr}[X_1, X_2]$ for each.

For each $\rho$, generate $\mathbf{Z}$ via Cholesky, transform to $\mathbf{U} = \Phi(\mathbf{Z})$, then to $\mathbf{X} = F^{-1}(\mathbf{U})$. The plot shows that the copula-induced correlation in $X$ is a monotone but nonlinear function of $\rho$.

In [8]:
# Part d: sweep rho from -1 to 1 using Cholesky
rhos = np.linspace(-1, 1, 21)
corr_x_vals = []
for r in rhos:
    Z1 = np.random.normal(0, 1, 10_000)
    if abs(r) == 1:
        # Degenerate case: Z2 = sign(r)*Z1 exactly
        Z_sweep = np.column_stack([Z1, np.sign(r) * Z1])
    else:
        Sigma_sweep = np.array([[1.0, r], [r, 1.0]])
        L_sweep = np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma_sweep)
        Z2 = r * Z1 + np.sqrt(1 - r**2) * np.random.normal(0, 1, 10_000)
        Z_sweep = np.column_stack([Z1, Z2])
    U_sweep = ndtr(Z_sweep)
    X_sweep = -np.log(1 - U_sweep)
    corr_x_vals.append(np.corrcoef(X_sweep.T)[0, 1])

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
plt.plot(rhos, corr_x_vals, 'o-')
plt.plot([-1, 1], [-1, 1], 'k--', label='y = x')
plt.xlabel(r"$\rho$ (correlation of $Z$)")
plt.ylabel(r"$\mathrm{Corr}[X_1, X_2]$")
plt.title("Exponential copula: Corr[X] vs $\\rho$")
plt.legend(); plt.grid(True); plt.show()

Problem 4¶

Consider a three-state, discrete time Markov chain with states $1$, $2$ and $3$ and transition matrix

$$P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.07 & 0.03 \\ 0.12 & 0.8 & 0.08 \\ 0.2 & 0.3 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$$

Part a¶

Generate one trajectory from $t = 0$ to $t = 100,000$ of this Markov chain and plot the first 500 time steps of the trajectory. (Generate the initial state from a uniform distribution.)

Part b¶

Use the full trajectory you calculated in part (a) to estimate the expected proportion of time spent in each state.

Part c¶

Calculate the dominant eigenvalue of $P$ and its corresponding left eigenvector. How does this eigenvector relate to the expected times you found in part (2)?

Solution

Parts a & b : Simulate the chain using the inverse transform method on each row of $P$.

At each step, draw $U \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$ and find the smallest $k$ such that $\sum_{j=1}^k P_{\text{state},j} \geq U$. This is equivalent to np.random.choice but uses only uniform primitives.

The initial state is drawn uniformly from $\{1,2,3\}$ via $\lfloor 3U \rfloor$.

In [9]:
P = np.array([[0.9,  0.07, 0.03],
              [0.12, 0.8,  0.08],
              [0.2,  0.3,  0.5 ]])

def next_state(current, P, u):
    """Inverse transform on discrete distribution row P[current]."""
    cdf = 0.0
    for k in range(P.shape[1]):
        cdf += P[current, k]
        if u <= cdf:
            return k
    return P.shape[1] - 1

n_steps = 100_000
states = np.zeros(n_steps + 1, dtype=int)

# Initial state uniform on {0,1,2} via inverse transform
u0 = np.random.uniform()
states[0] = int(u0 * 3)

# Generate trajectory using uniform draws + inverse transform
U = np.random.uniform(size=n_steps)
for t in range(n_steps):
    states[t + 1] = next_state(states[t], P, U[t])

# Part a: plot first 500 steps
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 3))
plt.step(range(501), states[:501] + 1)
plt.xlabel("Time step"); plt.ylabel("State")
plt.yticks([1, 2, 3])
plt.title("Markov chain trajectory (first 500 steps)")
plt.show()

# Part b: proportion of time in each state
print("Part b : Empirical proportion of time in each state:")
for s in range(3):
    print(f"  State {s+1}: {np.mean(states == s):.4f}")

Part b : Empirical proportion of time in each state:
  State 1: 0.5765
  State 2: 0.3348
  State 3: 0.0887

Part c : The stationary distribution $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ satisfies $\boldsymbol{\pi} P = \boldsymbol{\pi}$, i.e., it is the left eigenvector of $P$ corresponding to eigenvalue 1.

Equivalently, $P^T \boldsymbol{\pi} = \boldsymbol{\pi}$ (right eigenvector of $P^T$). For any irreducible, aperiodic Markov chain, the dominant eigenvalue is 1 and the corresponding normalized eigenvector gives the long-run fraction of time spent in each state.

In [10]:
# Part c: dominant eigenvalue and left eigenvector of P
# Left eigenvector: pi P = pi  <=>  P^T pi = pi
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(P.T)
idx = np.argmax(np.real(eigenvalues))
dominant_eigenvalue = np.real(eigenvalues[idx])
pi = np.real(eigenvectors[:, idx])
pi = pi / pi.sum()

print(f"Dominant eigenvalue: {dominant_eigenvalue:.6f}")
print(f"Stationary distribution: {pi.round(4)}")

Dominant eigenvalue: 1.000000
Stationary distribution: [0.5775 0.3343 0.0881]

Problem 5¶

Suppose $S\sim GBM(0.1, 0.3)$. In this problem, you will simulate $S_{t_k}$ at the times $t_k = 0.01k$ for $0 \leq k \leq 1000$. Use the initial condition $S_0 = 1$.

Part a¶

Simulate $S$ once and plot the trajectory.

Part b¶

Simulate $S$ at least $10,000$ times and plot the mean trajectory.

Part c¶

Estimate the probability that the maximum of $S_{t_k}$ is no greater than 6.

Part d¶

Estimate the probability that $S_{t_k}$ ever leaves the interval $[0.25, 10]$.

Solution

For $S \sim \mathrm{GBM}(\mu, \sigma)$, the exact discretization at times $t_k = k\,\Delta t$ is:

$$S_{t_{k+1}} = S_{t_k} \exp\!\left(\left(\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right)\Delta t + \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,Z_k\right), \quad Z_k \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1)$$

This is exact (not an approximation) because GBM has log-normal increments. The theoretical mean is $\mathbb{E}[S_t] = S_0 e^{\mu t}$.

In [11]:
mu_gbm, sigma_gbm, S0 = 0.1, 0.3, 1.0
dt, n_steps = 0.01, 1000
t = np.arange(n_steps + 1) * dt

def simulate_gbm(mu, sigma, S0, dt, n_steps):
    Z = np.random.normal(0, 1, n_steps)
    log_ret = (mu - 0.5 * sigma**2) * dt + sigma * np.sqrt(dt) * Z
    return S0 * np.exp(np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(log_ret)]))

# Part a: single trajectory
S_single = simulate_gbm(mu_gbm, sigma_gbm, S0, dt, n_steps)
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))
plt.plot(t, S_single)
plt.xlabel("t"); plt.ylabel("$S_t$")
plt.title("GBM single trajectory")
plt.show()

Part b : Simulate $10{,}000$ trajectories and plot the sample mean against the theoretical mean $\mathbb{E}[S_t] = e^{\mu t}$.

In [12]:
# Part b: 10,000 trajectories, mean trajectory
n_sim = 10_000
S_all = np.array([simulate_gbm(mu_gbm, sigma_gbm, S0, dt, n_steps) for _ in range(n_sim)])

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))
plt.plot(t, S_all.mean(axis=0), label="Sample mean")
plt.plot(t, S0 * np.exp(mu_gbm * t), '--', label=r"$E[S_t] = e^{\mu t}$")
plt.xlabel("t"); plt.ylabel("$S_t$")
plt.title("GBM mean trajectory (10,000 simulations)")
plt.legend(); plt.show()

Part c : Estimate $P(\max_{k} S_{t_k} \leq 6)$ as the fraction of trajectories whose maximum never exceeds 6.

Part d : Estimate $P(S_{t_k} \text{ ever leaves } [0.25, 10])$ as the fraction of trajectories that at some point fall below 0.25 or exceed 10.

In [13]:
# Part c: P(max(S_tk) <= 6)
max_S = S_all.max(axis=1)
prob_c = np.mean(max_S <= 6)
print(f"Part c : P(max S_tk <= 6) = {prob_c:.4f}")

# Part d: P(S ever leaves [0.25, 10])
leaves = np.any((S_all < 0.25) | (S_all > 10), axis=1)
prob_d = np.mean(leaves)
print(f"Part d : P(S leaves [0.25, 10]) = {prob_d:.4f}")

Part c : P(max S_tk <= 6) = 0.8522
Part d : P(S leaves [0.25, 10]) = 0.1020
